transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, um, nice to meet you too. I'm here because... well, it's my job, mostly. I mean, I guess it's happening all the time, but it's really, really bad at work, and it's getting dangerous. I'm a flagger, you know, for road construction and utility crews? I've been doing it for years. I actually have a bachelor's degree, but the flagging work gets me outside, and usually, it's just second nature, you just get into a rhythm with the traffic and the crew. 

But lately, I came in because my mind just... it keeps going completely blank. And I mean at the absolute worst possible times. It's terrifying. Like, I will be standing there on the asphalt, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms—which I have filled out a thousand times, literally, it's the exact same paperwork for every single site—or I'll be holding my stop-slow paddle, just staring at the sign, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. They just vanish from my head. I'll just stand there holding the paddle, and I know the cars are coming, and I know the crew is behind me, but there's just this heavy, empty fog in my brain where the instructions should be. It's like someone just pulled the plug on my brain right in the middle of a shift, and I'm just frozen trying to remember basic, everyday things, and I just... I can't think. I can't process any of it.
During these blank spells, are you still aware of what is happening around you?

Well, um, aware is... I don't really know how to answer that, to be honest. I mean, I'm not unconscious. I haven't passed out on the asphalt or anything like that. My eyes are open. But as for being actually aware? I'm not sure. 

Like, I can see things happening, but it's like I'm trapped behind a really thick pane of dirty glass. I can see the cars lined up—like the other day, there was this massive, bright red Ford F-150 just idling right at my stop point, and I could hear the engine rumbling, and I could smell the hot tar and the diesel exhaust from the excavator working behind me. I can feel the wind flapping my high-vis vest against my shoulder, and the sweat dripping under my hard hat. So the sights and sounds are definitely coming in. My senses are working. 

But I don't know if I'm actually processing any of it, if that makes sense. It all just turns into meaningless noise and shapes. I'll look at the STOP side of my paddle, and it's just a red octagon with white lines on it. The meaning of it, the context of where I am and what I'm supposed to do with it, is just... gone. So I really don't know if you'd call that being aware. I'm just stuck in this heavy, awful fog, standing in the middle of the road, trying to force my brain to connect the dots, and it just won't. So, I don't know. I guess I'm there physically, the world is happening around me, but mentally, I just couldn't tell you what I'm actually comprehending when the fog rolls in.
How long does a typical blank spell last from beginning to end?

I honestly... I couldn't tell you an exact number. I mean, it's so incredibly hard to gauge time when you're in that state. Because, you know, when you're out there on the road, time is usually measured by the traffic flow, right? Like, you wait for the pilot car to come back around, or you count the cars in the queue. Usually, a standard hold is maybe three to five minutes depending on the work zone. 

But when this fog hits my brain... it feels like an absolute eternity. It feels like I've been standing there for hours, just completely paralyzed, staring at the pavement or the bumper of a car. But then, on the other hand, it might only be a few seconds? Because usually, nobody has started honking at me yet, and my foreman hasn't yelled at me over the two-way radio to flip my sign. So I'll sort of come back online, and that same red truck is still idling right there in front of me, so logically, it couldn't have been *that* long. 

But I just have absolutely no concept of the minutes passing. I mean, I wear a watch, a digital one so it's easy to read in the glare of the sun, but during those spells, I can't even formulate the thought to look at my wrist, let alone calculate when the blankness started and when it stopped. It's just a complete void. So whether it's ten seconds or two minutes, I really have absolutely no idea. It just feels like time stops completely, and I'm suspended in this awful, heavy nothingness, and I just... I wish I could give you a better answer, I really do, but I just don't know.

{"intent":"Determine whether the episodes involve impaired responsiveness suggestive of focal seizures","question":"When someone speaks to you during one of these blank spells, do you respond appropriately?\"}

I... well, see, that's another thing that's so hard to pin down. Because, like I was saying, it's usually just me and the traffic, right? The crew is usually further down the lane, maybe a hundred feet, maybe a quarter mile depending on the closure. So most of the time, nobody is actually right next to me trying to have a conversation. 

But, okay, there was this one time last week. I was working a water main repair job on Elm Street, right near the elementary school, so we had to be extra careful because of the kids and the buses. And I was standing there, and the fog rolled in, that heavy blankness. And I vaguely, distantly heard my radio crackle on my shoulder. It was Dave, my foreman. He's this big guy, always talks really loud, always kind of sounds like he's yelling even when he's just asking if anyone wants coffee from the gas station. 

So the radio crackled, and I could hear his voice, but it was like... it was like he was speaking a completely foreign language. Or like when adults talk in those old Charlie Brown cartoons, you know? Just that *wah-wah-wah* sound. I knew it was Dave, and I knew it was my radio, but the actual words? They just bounced right off me. I stood there staring at the radio on my shoulder, just looking at the little black antenna, and I couldn't figure out what to do with it. I couldn't reach up and press the button to talk back. I couldn't process what he was asking me—I think he was asking if the pilot car had cleared my end yet. 

So I didn't respond. I just stood there. And then a few seconds later, or maybe a minute later, I don't know, he yelled my name really loud over the radio—"Hey, you copy?!"—and that sort of snapped me out of it. And then I felt this horrible rush of panic, and I fumbled with the button and just said, "Yeah, copy," even though I had no idea what he had originally said. I just had to say something so he wouldn't come marching down the lane to see what was wrong with me. 

So I guess... no? I don't respond appropriately. Or I don't respond at all, really. It's just so terrifying because if a driver asked me a question, or if someone yelled to get out of the way of a backing dump truck... I just don't know if I'd be able to process it and react in time. The words just don't make sense when I'm in that state.
After one of these spells ends, do you notice confusion, unusual movements, or a period when you cannot remember what happened?

Um, no... no, not really. I mean, when it lifts, when that heavy fog finally breaks, it’s almost like... like coming up for air? But I wouldn't say I'm confused. Like, I know exactly who I am, and I know I’m standing in the middle of a work zone holding a STOP paddle. I know I’m on Elm Street, or Route 9, or wherever they have me stationed that day. It’s not like I wake up and look around going, "Where am I? How did I get here?" It’s nothing like that. 

And as for movements... no, definitely not. I'm not twitching or shaking or doing anything bizarre. If anything, I’m just completely rigid. Like, when I snap out of it, I’ll realize I’ve been gripping the aluminum pole of my sign so hard that my hands are cramping and my knuckles are completely white. But I’m not, you know, flailing around or doing anything that would make the crew or the drivers think I'm having some kind of physical fit. 

And I don't forget what happened, either. I mean, obviously, I couldn't process the radio or the time passing *during* the spell, like I told you, but I remember the actual experience of being stuck in that blankness. I remember staring at the grill of that red Ford F-150. I remember the exact feeling of the panic setting in when Dave yelled my name. There's no missing time where my brain just wiped the tape clean. I remember being trapped in it.

It’s really just... the aftermath is mostly just this overwhelming, crushing exhaustion. Like, my heart will be pounding out of my chest because I'm terrified I messed up the traffic pattern, and then this really dark, heavy dread just settles right into my bones. I'll just stand there thinking about how broken my brain is, and how I'm out here breathing in exhaust fumes and I can't even rely on my own mind to stay present. But as far as what you're asking? No confusion, no weird movements, and no amnesia. I just go right back to being aware, just... a much more terrified, exhausted version of myself, desperately hoping nobody noticed I was gone.
Do these blank spells ever happen when you are away from work and feeling relaxed?

Well, I mean... if I'm at home, just sitting on my couch, maybe watching a show or trying to read a book, and my mind goes blank, it doesn't really register the same way, you know? Because the stakes are so low. If I just kind of zone out while I'm making a sandwich, it just means I stand in the kitchen for a while. It's not a big deal. 

But the whole reason I actually came in to see a doctor in the first place is because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. The highest stakes times. Like, I will be standing right there on the job site, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms—which I have to fill out and sign every single time we set up a new work zone—or I'll be holding my stop-slow paddle, just staring at the big red letters... and suddenly I cannot remember the steps I have done for years. 

It's like someone just pulled the plug on my brain. I have a Bachelor's degree, you know? I'm an educated woman. I shouldn't be looking at a basic municipal safety form or a piece of aluminum on a stick and feeling like I've never seen it before in my life. But the thoughts just completely vanish. The procedures, the safety steps, everything I know how to do just disappears, and I'm left staring at this paddle trying to remember how my own job works. 

So... maybe it happens when I'm relaxed? I don't know, maybe. It's hard to say. But it's those moments at work, when I'm looking at that paddle or those forms and I can't remember what to do with them, that just completely terrify me. That's what really pushed me to get help, because I can't keep losing my train of thought and forgetting basic steps when people's safety is on the line. It's just so incredibly frustrating.
Does the fear or panic start before your mind goes blank, or does it begin only after the blankness has already started?

I... well, no, definitely not before. It’s not like a warning bell goes off, you know? If I had some kind of warning, like if I started feeling anxious or panicked *before* it happened, maybe I could radio Dave and say, "Hey, I need to step off the asphalt for a second," or I could at least lean against the pilot car so I'm not just standing out in the open. But there's no warning. It’s just... the fog rolls in. 

The panic really only sets in once I'm already in it, or honestly, mostly when I'm snapping out of it. Like I was saying about that time on Elm Street, or when I'm looking at those closure forms. The blankness is already there, already happening. And then it’s like this slow, creeping horror when I realize I can’t process anything, or when I snap back and realize I've just been completely checked out. That’s when my heart starts hammering against my ribs. 

It’s the realization that I was just a sitting duck out there. I mean, you have to understand the environment we work in. You’ve got people texting and driving, people who are furious that their morning commute is delayed by road work, massive heavy-duty trucks hauling trailers flying past you at forty miles an hour in a twenty-five zone. We've had cones run over, we've had side mirrors clip our vests. It is not a safe place to be if you aren't paying attention. 

So the fear isn't what causes the blankness, and it doesn't warn me it's coming. The fear is entirely about the fact that my brain just went offline while I'm standing feet away from moving traffic. It's the aftermath. It's the sudden, terrifying realization of how vulnerable I was, and how I could have gotten myself or one of my crew members killed because I couldn't remember how to flip a piece of aluminum from STOP to SLOW. So, no, it's definitely not before. It's only after the blankness has already started, or after it breaks, that the sheer terror of what just happened actually hits me.
Has anyone ever watched one of these blank spells from start to finish, and if so, what did they observe you doing?

Well, I think... actually, Dave, our foreman who I mentioned earlier, he's probably the one who has seen it happen the most clearly from the outside. And it all goes back to exactly what I was telling you a few minutes ago, about the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. Because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the absolute worst, most critical times. Like when I’m staring at those road-closure forms or looking at my paddle and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. When that happens, when all my thoughts just completely evaporate and I lose my grip on what I'm supposed to be doing, Dave has actually been watching me from across the work zone.

He told me later that he thought I was just daydreaming or ignoring him at first. He said he watched me just stop moving altogether. According to him, I just looked like a statue. I was standing there, feet planted, gripping the aluminum pole, just staring dead ahead at the grill of a truck or down at the asphalt. He said I didn't look like I was having a medical emergency or anything, I just looked entirely vacant. Like nobody was home. He tried waving his arms at me from the paver, and when I didn't wave back or flip my sign to let the pilot car through, he realized something was off. 

That's when he had to start yelling my name over the noise of the diesel engines and the traffic. And to him, he just saw me suddenly flinch and blink hard and snap out of it. But for me, it was that horrible realization that I had just been standing there with an entirely empty head, completely forgetting how to do my job while people were depending on me. It’s so incredibly humiliating, you know? Because I am an educated person, and to have my crew watch me just short-circuit and forget basic safety procedures... it’s just awful. They don't see the panic on the inside while it's happening, they just see me freeze up and stare into space until someone yells loud enough to break the fog. So, yes, Dave has watched it happen from start to finish, and to him it just looks like I've completely checked out of reality and forgotten where I am, which is exactly why I had to come get help. I can't have people watching me fail at my job like that.
When Dave watched one of these episodes, approximately how long did you remain still and unresponsive before you snapped out of it?

Well, Dave told me it was probably only about forty-five seconds to a minute. Which, I mean, if you're just sitting in a doctor's office or in your living room watching TV, a minute is nothing, right? You blink and a minute is gone. But out there on the asphalt, with commuters flying by and heavy diesel machinery operating just a few feet away, a minute is an absolute eternity. A truck going forty miles an hour travels a very long way in sixty seconds. 

So to Dave, it was just a minute of me standing there like a statue. But for me... and I know I keep coming back to this, but I really need you to understand because it is the entire reason I came in to see you in the first place—my mind just keeps going blank at the absolute worst, most dangerous times. During that minute, it’s not like I’m just daydreaming about a vacation or trying to figure out what to make for dinner. I will look down at the road-closure forms on my clipboard, or I'll be looking right at my stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's just... gone. The knowledge is just entirely wiped away for that entire sixty seconds. 

And it's so unbelievably frustrating because, like I said, I have a Bachelor's degree. I am not a stupid woman. I know how to do my job. But for that minute, or however long it actually is, I am just completely empty. Dave says I just freeze up, but he doesn't understand that I'm literally looking at a piece of aluminum on a stick and having absolutely no concept of what it's used for or what my job even is. 

And then, you know, he finally yells loud enough over the paver, and I flinch, and I snap back into reality. The sixty seconds is over. But the fact that it happens at all... that I can just lose years of procedural memory while I'm supposed to be the one directing live traffic and keeping my crew safe... it's just completely unacceptable. It's terrifying. So, yeah, he said about a minute, maybe a little less, but a minute is all it takes for someone to get killed out there if I'm not doing my job.
Have you ever had one of these blank spells while you were relaxed at home, with no work-related pressure or danger around you?

No... no, not really. I mean, if I'm just sitting on my couch at home, you know, maybe watching a game show or folding laundry, or just doing things where it really doesn't matter if I zone out for a second—it doesn't happen like that. And I know I keep repeating myself, doctor, I know I sound like a broken record today, but I just really need to make sure you understand because it is the entire crux of why I'm sitting in this chair. 

I came in to get help specifically because my mind keeps going completely blank at the absolute worst, most critical times. It's never when I'm safe in my living room where nothing bad can happen. It's always, always when the pressure is on and I absolutely have to be present. Like I've been saying, I'll be out there on the asphalt, staring down at those road-closure forms, or I'll have that stop-slow paddle gripped in my hands with a line of angry commuters waiting on me, and suddenly... I just cannot remember the steps I have done for years. 

It's like someone just takes an eraser to my brain, but only when it is most dangerous for that to happen. If this was just happening at home while I was reading a book or something, I honestly wouldn't even be here. I'd probably just think I was getting a little older, or maybe just overtired from the long shifts. But it's the fact that I lose all my procedural memory, all that basic knowledge of how to do my job, right when people's lives are literally in my hands. That's the part I can't live with. So, no, it's not when I'm relaxed with no pressure. It's exactly the opposite, which is why it's so terrifying.
Do these blank spells occur only in situations involving work-related pressure, or have they ever happened during another kind of stressful situation?

Well, you know, I’ve actually spent a lot of time trying to figure that out myself. I sit there and try to analyze it, trying to find a pattern. Because I ask myself, is it just the job? Is it the noise of the traffic? But really, when I break it down, it comes down to the stakes involved. My life outside of work is pretty quiet, honestly. I don't have a lot of high-stakes drama or emergencies happening in my personal life, so I don't really have those same intense pressure-cooker moments at home or at the grocery store or running errands. 

But the core issue—and I know I am sounding incredibly repetitive today, doctor, I really do apologize for looping back to this again, but it is just so vital that you see the full picture—I came in here to see you because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the absolute worst, most critical times. 

So, while it happens at work, it's because work is where the pressure is. Work is where people can get hurt if I mess up. If I had that kind of life-or-death stress happening somewhere else, I am almost certain it would happen there, too. Because it's the pressure that does it. The pressure spikes, and then, just like I was explaining earlier, I will look right at the road-closure forms on my clipboard, or I'll be gripping that stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's just a total, catastrophic loss of my procedural memory right when the stress is at its absolute peak. 

So, to answer your question, it manifests during work-related pressure because that's where my stress is concentrated, but the fundamental problem is just that my brain completely shuts down whenever the worst possible moment arrives, regardless of the specific location. It’s just... it’s unbearable living with this constant fear that the next time things get stressful, my brain is just going to abandon me again.
During a blank spell, do your surroundings ever feel unreal or dreamlike, as though you are separated from the world around you?

Dreamlike? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s not like I’m floating above my body or, you know, trapped in some kind of weird movie or a dream where things get all fuzzy and distorted. The world around me is actually incredibly real, painfully real, even when my brain just completely stops working. I can still feel the heat radiating off the fresh asphalt through the soles of my work boots, and I can still hear the deafening roar of the milling machine or the paver right behind me. It doesn't fade away into the background like things do when you're dreaming. The smell of the diesel exhaust is still right there burning my nose. 

So I'm very much physically present in the world. I'm not separated from my surroundings at all. But... and I know I'm probably talking your ear off today, and I know I've said this a dozen times already, but it's just so hard to articulate exactly how terrifying this is—it's not the world that disappears, it's my own mind. It's my understanding of what I'm doing in that world. 

I'm standing there, fully anchored to the pavement, looking at the exact same things I always look at, but the procedural memory, the basic knowledge of why I am holding a stop-slow paddle or what a road-closure form even is... that's what vanishes. So it's not a dream. If it felt like a dream, maybe it wouldn't be so scary because you know you'll wake up. But because everything is so incredibly real, and I know I'm standing in a live traffic lane with massive trucks barreling toward me, and I suddenly have absolutely zero idea how to keep myself or my crew safe... that is an actual, living nightmare. It's happening in reality. So, no, to answer your question, I don't feel disconnected from my surroundings. I just feel completely disconnected from my own brain, right when I need it the most.
During a blank spell, can you deliberately move or speak if you try hard to do so?

Well, physically? Yes, I mean, I'm not... I'm not paralyzed or frozen stiff like a statue or anything like that. My muscles still work just fine. If I needed to just blindly run away, I suppose my legs would carry me, and I can physically open my mouth and make sounds. My vocal cords aren't broken. But... it's like, what good is being able to move or speak if the instruction manual in your head is just completely gone? 

I can try hard to speak, sure, but what am I supposed to say when I've completely forgotten the radio codes? Or when I don't even remember who I'm supposed to be calling on the walkie-talkie? I could wave my arms around, I could flip that stop-slow paddle back and forth all day long because my hands still function, but because my mind is just a total, terrifying blank, I wouldn't know which side of the paddle is supposed to be facing the oncoming traffic. 

And that’s the thing, doctor, and I know I am just talking in circles today and taking up so much of your time, but this is the crux of it all. It’s almost worse that I can move, because I’m standing there, fully capable of doing my job physically, but the mental part—the procedural memory of how to do it safely—is just wiped clean. So, yes, to answer your question, I can deliberately move my body and I can speak words if I force myself to, but it doesn't help me at all because the knowledge directing those movements is just... it's just vanished. It's like having a fully gassed-up truck with no steering wheel. The engine runs, but you have absolutely no idea how to drive it anymore. That's exactly what it feels like.
Are these blank spells nearly identical each time, with the same pattern from one episode to the next?

Well, that's... I mean, that's a really good question, and I've spent a lot of time analyzing it, trying to see if there's a specific pattern, like a sequence of events that happens exactly the same way every single time. Because if there was a pattern, maybe I could predict it, you know? Maybe I could feel it coming on and step away from the traffic lane before it fully hits. But... honestly, I'm not really sure if they are completely identical every single time. 

It's hard to say because, well, when it happens, I'm in such a state of sheer panic. The core of it—the part where my mind just completely empties out and I forget everything I'm supposed to be doing—that part feels the same. That terrifying feeling of the instruction manual just vanishing from my brain, that's always there. But as for the exact pattern from one episode to the next... I haven't really noticed if it starts with the same thought or if it lasts the exact same amount of seconds. 

Sometimes I'm holding the paddle, sometimes I'm looking at the paperwork, sometimes the truck is fifty yards away, sometimes it's right on top of me. So the circumstances around it change, and because I'm just so overwhelmed by the sudden blankness, I can't really tell you if the internal experience follows an identical step-by-step pattern every time. I just know that the end result is always the same catastrophic loss of knowing how to do my job. I'm sorry, I know I'm probably not giving you a very clear answer, and I know I just keep talking and talking, but it's just so hard to analyze the exact pattern of something that essentially erases my ability to think while it's happening.
If someone gently touched your shoulder during one of these spells, would you respond to them?

I... well, I don't really know for sure, because, to be completely honest with you, no one has actually ever touched my shoulder while it's happening. I mean, usually when I'm out there on the job, I'm standing by myself at my post, right? The rest of the crew is either down the road operating the heavy machinery or they're in the pilot car, so I'm physically isolated from everyone else most of the time. There's no one close enough to just reach out and tap me on the shoulder. 

But if I really think about it... if someone did walk up to me and touch my shoulder while my mind was in that completely blank state... I imagine I would probably jump out of my skin. Because, like I was saying before, my senses are still working. I can still feel things. So a hand on my shoulder would definitely register physically. I wouldn't just ignore it or not feel it. But as to how I would actually respond to them? I really couldn't tell you. 

Would I turn around and be able to speak to them normally? Probably not, because the instruction manual in my head is still gone. I might just stare at them in a total panic. Or maybe the shock of being touched would snap me out of it? I don't know. I've spent so many hours lying awake at night, just running these scenarios over and over in my head, trying to figure out how to handle this, how to make it stop, and I just... I don't have the answers. And I know I'm probably frustrating you by not giving you a simple yes or no, and I apologize for just rambling on again, but without it actually happening, I really have no way of knowing if a touch would bring me back to reality or just terrify me even more. I just haven't experienced it.
After an episode ends, can you remember everything that happened during the spell, or is there a period you cannot recall?

I... well, I really don't know for sure. I mean, I've tried so hard to piece it all together afterward, you know? Like, I'll be standing there, and the panic starts to recede just a little bit, and I realize I'm back in my body, back in reality, and the very first thing I do is try to rewind the tape in my head. I try to go back and figure out exactly what just happened, second by second. But... it's like trying to remember a dream right after you wake up, where the edges are all blurry and you know you were just experiencing something incredibly intense, but the actual details are just slipping through your fingers like sand.

I remember the feeling, of course. I remember that absolute, crushing terror of not knowing what to do with the paddle, or not knowing the radio codes, like I was telling you before. I remember the sensation of my mind going completely blank. But as for the actual events? Like, did a specific car pass by while I was frozen? Did I shift my weight from one foot to the other? Did the wind blow? I honestly couldn't tell you. 

It's not like I black out completely and wake up on the ground or anything. I know I was standing there the whole time. But there's definitely a gap, or at least a really thick fog, over the actual minutes that pass while I'm in that state. It’s so incredibly frustrating, doctor, because I feel like if I could just remember exactly what was happening around me during the spell, maybe I could figure out what’s triggering it. I spend hours analyzing every single shift I work, trying to fill in those gaps, trying to remember if maybe a certain color of car drove by, or if the radio crackled in a specific way, but the memory just isn't there. It's just... missing. And I know I'm taking up so much time explaining this, and I'm probably not giving you the exact clinical answer you need, but I just don't know if I remember everything or not. It's all just a terrifying blur.
During a spell, have you ever been observed making repetitive movements such as lip-smacking, chewing, swallowing, or picking at your clothes?

I... well, no, I don't think so. I mean, like I said, I'm usually out there all alone, so there's not really anyone around to observe me, you know? The crew is too far away to see what my mouth or my hands are doing. But even if they were close... I really don't think I do any of those things. 

I've thought about this a lot, too, trying to imagine what I must look like to someone driving past. I mean, do I look crazy? Do I look like I'm having some kind of fit? But honestly, I think I just look like a statue. Because when that blankness hits, and the panic just floods my entire system, I feel like I'm completely frozen. It's like every muscle in my body just locks up because my brain is screaming at me that I don't know what to do next. 

So, no, I've never noticed myself chewing on anything, or smacking my lips, or picking at my safety vest or my clothes. I'm usually gripping that stop paddle so hard my knuckles probably turn white, just completely rigid, staring straight ahead while my mind is just... gone. I mean, I guess it's possible I might swallow hard because my mouth goes dry from the fear, but as for like, a repetitive movement? Like doing it over and over again? No, I really don't think so. It's more of a complete and total paralysis. I just stand there, trapped inside my own head, until it finally passes. I'm sorry, I know I'm probably giving you way more detail than you need again, but I just want to make sure you have the whole picture of what's happening to me out there.
When Dave called your name loudly and you snapped out of the spell, were you immediately able to understand him and respond normally?

Dave? I... wait, I'm sorry, doctor, I'm a little confused by that. I don't... I don't think I ever mentioned a Dave? I mean, there is a Dave who works for the contracting company, he drives the pilot car on Tuesdays and Thursdays usually, but... he's never actually yelled my name during one of my spells. 

Like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, I'm completely isolated out there on the asphalt. Nobody has ever been close enough to shout at me or snap me out of it. I'm so sorry if I said something earlier that made it sound like that happened, because I really try to be as accurate as possible when I'm describing all this to you. I spend so much time overthinking every single detail of my shifts, just agonizing over what happened and what didn't happen, so I'm fairly certain I would remember if Dave, or anyone else for that matter, had yelled at me to snap me out of that blank state. 

But since it hasn't happened, I really don't have an answer for whether I'd understand him or respond normally. I imagine it would be just like the shoulder-touching scenario we just talked about—I'd probably just be frozen there, gripping my stop paddle, completely panicked and unable to process the words right away because the instruction manual in my head is still missing.
